power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Accurate vessel segmentaLon is essenLal for reliable hemodynamic quanLficaLon in 4D Flow MRI.

Automated segmentaLon with deep learning offers a promising alternaLve to the Lmeconsuming, operator-dependent manual segmentaLon, but its applicaLon is oeen hindered by the scarcity of labeled datasets.

Moreover, while a previous study has evaluated the impact of automated vs manual segmentaLon on downstream intracranial hemodynamic quanLficaLon, it remains to be explored whether variability between different automated segmentaLon methods affects hemodynamic quanLficaLon significantly, parLcularly in the context of intracranial 7T 4D Flow MRI.
We invesLgated a transfer learning-based intracranial artery segmentaLon model using a 3D full-resoluLon nnU-Net, pretrained on 355 TOF-MRA scans and fine-tuned on 11 7T 4D Flow MRI scans.

The model was compared with two published models: a direct-transfer U-Net pretrained only on TOF-MRA without 4D Flow MRI fine-tuning, and a DenseNet U-Net trained from scratch on the same 11 7T 4D Flow MRI scans.
SegmentaLon performance was evaluated against the manual reference on test sets with different resoluLons and the impact on downstream hemodynamic quanLficaLon was assessed.

The transfer learning-based nnU-Net achieved the highest Dice score (>0.85), the lowest HD95 (~3 mm), and the highest ICCs in cross-secLonal area (0.62-0.87, except PCAs) and mean blood flow (0.78-0.98).

text.text: To address this gap, we adopt a transfer learning-based intracranial artery segmentaLon strategy for 4D Flow MRI, built upon the nnU-Net framework.
This model was pre-trained on a large dataset of brain TOF-MRA images and fine-tuned on a smaller 4D Flow MRI dataset.

The finetuned model was then evaluated against the manual reference and compared with two previously published intracranial artery segmentaLon models, one pretrained on TOF-MRA and the other trained from scratch using the same 4D Flow MRI dataset used for fine-tuning, to assess segmentaLon performance across different acquisiLon protocols and spaLal resoluLons.

Furthermore, we evaluated how the different segmentaLon methods affect the quanLficaLon of 4D Flow MRI-derived hemodynamic parameters, providing insights into the extent of variability introduced by segmentaLon differences.

text.text: Briefly, vessel surfaces were extracted from the segmentaLon masks and smoothed using Laplacian filtering with 15 iteraLons and a step size of λ = 0.1.
For each surface vertex, the local radius was esLmated from the nearest intersecLon with the opposite vessel surface along the inward wall-normal direcLon.
Velocity values were then sampled along the inward wall-normal direcLon at three equidistant points, corresponding to one-third, two-thirds, and the full local radius from the vessel wall.

Velocity values at off-grid sampling locaLons were obtained using natural-neighbor interpolaLon based on a Delaunay triangulaLon of the velocity grid, with the vessel wall assigned zero velocity to impose a no-slip boundary condiLon.

Aeer rotaLng the local coordinate system to align the wall normal with the z-axis, the tangenLal velocity components were fixed with smoothing splines along the normal direcLon with weights of [0.1, 1, 1, 1] and an adapLve tolerance of max(|vₜ|)/100, where vₜ denotes the sampled tangenLal velocity profile.

The nnU-Net ablaLon experiments further clarified the role of TOF-MRA pre-training and 4D Flow MRI fine-tuning.

Although both modaliLes are flow-sensiLve, TOF-MRA primarily relies on inflowrelated enhancement, whereas 4D Flow MRI-derived PCMRA combines magnitude and velocity informaLon, potenLally highlighLng addiLonal vascular structures, including veins and extracranial vessels.

Furthermore, TOF-MRA retains some anatomical background informaLon from staLonary brain Lssue despite RF saturaLon, while PCMRA largely suppresses staLonary Lssue signals, resulLng in less visible anatomical background structures.
These differences in both vascular appearance and surrounding Lssue contrast may affect the transferability of learned features between the two modaliLes.

Indeed, visual inspecLon of the direct-transfer nnU-Net predicLons suggested that some segmentaLon errors arose from false-posiLve predicLons of non-target vascular structures rather than inaccurate delineaLon of intracranial arteries alone.
These observaLons may partly explain why TOF-MRA pre-training alone was insufficient for direct applicaLon to 4D Flow MRI and why domain-specific fine-tuning improved segmentaLon performance.

With all 11 training cases, the from-scratch nnU-Net achieved slightly bexer mean Dice and HD95 on the low-resoluLon test set, whereas the fine-tuned nnU-Net performed bexer on the high-resoluLon test set.

Since fine-tuning was performed exclusively on low-resoluLon 4D Flow MRI, this suggests that TOF-MRA pre-training may have improved generalizaLon to acquisiLon se}ngs not represented in the fine-tuning data.
However, this benefit cannot be axributed to spaLal resoluLon alone, as the low-and high-resoluLon datasets also differed in VENC and other acquisiLon parameters.
The fine-tuned nnU-Net also showed more stable performance on the high-resoluLon test set when fewer training cases were available.

In addiLon, extending from-scratch training from 200 to 1000 epochs did not consistently improve performance, parLcularly on the high-resoluLon test set, suggesLng that longer training alone may not improve robustness in limited-data se}ngs.
Together, these findings suggest that TOF-MRA pre-training followed by 4D Flow MRI fine-tuning may help achieve robust segmentaLon performance with limited 4D Flow MRI annotaLons.

Because these ablaLon experiments used a single nested subset sequence without repeated random sampling, the observed robustness across reduced fine-tuning subsets should be interpreted as exploratory.

In addiLon to this robustness, the study-specific subgroup analysis suggests potenLal generalizability across acquisiLon protocols, as the fine-tuned nnU-Net showed more stable performance across the Flow@Aneurysm and DETAILING subsets than the DenseNet U-Net and from-scratch nnU-Net.

Blood flow is pulsaLle, and intracranial arteries are compliant, changing their lumen throughout the cardiac cycle, whereas the manual reference used in our analysis was derived from a Lme-averaged PCMRA image that cannot capture phase-specific vessel geometry.

Although the segmentaLon models could in principle generate Lme-resolved masks, producing a Lme-resolved manual reference would require frame-by-frame manual annotaLon and extensive quality control, which is impracLcal.

In addiLon, because centerlines and analysis planes were generated separately for each segmentaLon, the observed hemodynamic differences may reflect both vessel segmentaLon differences and variability introduced by plane placement.
However, this approach reflects a realisLc downstream workflow, and variability was minimized as much as possible by selecLng analysis planes at corresponding anatomical locaLons across methods.

In addiLon, QVT-based flow analysis was restricted to vessel segments that could be successfully analyzed across all four segmentaLon pipelines, the reported agreement may be overesLmated and does not account for segmentaLon or analysis failures.

Furthermore, parLal-volume effects and flow-related signal loss cause uncertainty in both the vessel boundary and the near-wall velocity gradient, thereby affecLng not only segmentaLon accuracy but also WSS esLmaLon.

Therefore, both manual and automated PCMRAbased segmentaLons can deviate from the physical vessel wall, and the reported WSS agreement should be interpreted as agreement relaLve to the reference segmentaLon.

Second, the comparison with baseline models should be interpreted as a pipeline-level comparison rather than a fully architecture-matched comparison.
This design was moLvated by the available implementaLons of the baseline models and by our aim to preserve their published or default se}ngs as much as possible.
Therefore, the evaluated baseline models differed not only in architecture but also in training strategy and preprocessing pipeline.

Third, future studies could include topology-aware metrics, such as clDice, or centerline-based measures to bexer evaluate vessel connecLvity and small-branch preservaLon in branching vascular trees.

Therefore, future work should evaluate whether the transfer-learning strategy can be adapted to 3T 4D Flow MRI through dedicated fine-tuning on representaLve clinical datasets.
